full_judgment:
43. 10.00: File of Crl. Misc. Petition No. 280 of 2006 sent by DM, Chittagong: Pursuant to order dated 10.09.2014 passed by this Court, the District Magistrate, Chittagong has sent the original file of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 280 of 2006 in which the bail order allegedly passed in Criminal Appeal No. 1409 of 2006 was processed for the purpose of acceptance of the bail bond. 

 50. 12.03: The original record of Special Tribunal Case No. 759 of 1999 shows that it arose form an allegation of an offence under the Arms Act, 1878 and respondent No.7 was one of the accused persons. This record reveals the details of the position of his custody, his appearance in court and bail during the period of 10.10.2001 to 06.06.2006 in that case. This record shows that he was in custody up to 31.05.2006. 

 (a) that although in the Cause Title and at some places of the text of the Writ Petition, the expression “public interest litigation” has been used, the dispute raised in this case and the Rule nisi issued by this court are in the nature which, in English law, is called a writ of quo warranto, 

 (a) that in the Cause Title and in the body of the Writ Petition (para-3), the petitioner has himself described this case as a “public interest litigation” (shortly PIL) and that it involves a question of great public importance, namely the validity of the election of respondent No. 7 as declared by the appropriate constitutional body, being the Election Commission and therefore this Writ Petition has to be judged by the principles applicable to a PIL, and 

 71. 17.04: But I fail to accept the submission of Mr. Ahmed that the expression “public interest litigation” as used in the Cause Title or in a paragraph of the Writ Petition has rendered this case to be a public interest litigation. Such sporadic references to that expression are not the determinant factors for deciding the nature of the case. The determinant factors are the issues raised in the Writ Petition in relation to the particular fact (s) and the standing of the petitioner. 

 “Broadly stated, the quo warrant proceeding affords a judicial remedy by which any person, who holds an independent substantive public office, or franchise, or liberty, is called upon to show by what right he holds the said office, franchise or liberty; so that his title to it may be duly determined and in case finding is that the holder of the office has no title to it, he would be ousted from that office by judicial order------------.” 

 110. 21.00: On this issue, the incumbent MP claims that he was released on 01.12.2005. On the contrary the contrary the Jail authorities claim that he was realeased on 01.06.2006. The incumbent MP relies on two documents, namely Annexure-1 being the photocopy of a Register, which has also been filed by Prothom Alo as Annexure-5, and the Rejoinder issued by the Senior Jail Super named Md. Sagir. The photocopy and original thereof are on record as Annexure-2 and 7. 

 126. 21.16: The above report of the IG Prison about the date of release of the incumbent MP on 01.06.2006 is consistent with the original file of Cr. Misc. Petition No. 280 of 2006 of the office of the District Magistrate (DM), Chittagong which was called for by this court. This file reveals the following scenario: 

 127. 21.17: The reports made by the Senior Jail Super and the IG, Prison that incumbent MP was in jail after 01.12.2005 and up to 01.06.2006 is further supported by the original judicial record of Special Tribunal Case No. 759 of 1999 (GR No. 129 of 1991 corresponding to Double Mooring P.S. Case No. 24(1) 1991) of the Special Tribunal (Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Court No. 4, Chittagong. Pursuant to the order of this court, that record was produced by the office of this Court as available in the office in connection Misc Case No. 15077 of 2014 arising from the said case No. 759 of 1999 in which the incumbent MP is one of the accused persons. 

 128. 21.18: The original record of Special Tribunal Case No. 759 of 1999 reveals the following scenario: 

 22.00: The documents relied on by the jail authorities, namely (1) the report of the Senior Jail Super Sagir Mia (Respondent No. 9) denying the correctness of the Rejoinder dated 10.05.2014 (Annexure 1) issued by himself ,and the documents in support of his denial and (2) the reports of the IG Prison along with other Jail documents including the Release Diary, (3) the contents of the original file of Misc Petition No. 280 of 2006 of the DM, Chittagong, no doubt establish the fact of release of the incumbent MP on 01.06.2006. 

 140. 23.01: Deliberation: On this Issue, Mr. Shafique Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the incumbent MP, submits that, according to section 35A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Cr.P.C) deduction of the period of the pre-judgment custody of an accused from the sentence of imprisonment imposed on him is mandatory and therefore the incumbent MP is entitled to that benefit. 

 24.00: In view of the above, it is held that the incumbent MP is not entitled to the deduction of the pre-judgment custody period of 143 days as claimed by him. Accordingly Issue No. 4 is decided in the negative i.e. against the incumbent MP. 

 (a) according to rule 766 of the Jail Code, Special Remission can be awarded on yearly basis, by the Superintendent up to a maximum of 30 days and by the Government up to 60 days, but no document has been produced by the incumbent MP or by the Jail authorities about such Remission and therefore he is not entitled to Special Remission, 

 (a) Chapter XXI of the Jail Code, particularly rules 756 to 760, provide for allowing Ordinary Remission and Special Remission. Moreover rule 689 further provides for Remission on account of Festival days, and Public holidays, and Gazetted holidays and thus, under the said rules, the incumbent MP is entitled to three types of remission and the total quantum thereof stand as follows: General Remission - 557 days+Special Remission - 343 days+ Festival, holiday etc – 651 days = Total = 1551 days. 

 (c) The Certificate of সন্ধানী (Annexure X-4) about blood donation by the incumbent MP on 13 dates is to be taken as correct and thus he, according to those Circulars, is entitled to a remission of 486 days and the total remission earned by him stands at 1551+486=2037 days. 

 (09) Rule 782 generally prohibits engaging a convict sentenced to rigorous imprisonment to work on “Sundays” and “the gazetted holidays” as specified by rule 689. However as stated earlier Rule 759 allows engaging certain convicts to work as cooks, sweeper etc on Sundays and holidays, and they are entitled to remission of three days of ordinary remission in a Quarter (i.e. 3 months), in addition to other remission. 

 175. 30.03: So from the scheme of the of Jail Code considered as a whole, particularly rule 689 specifying the holidays, and rule 782 generally prohibiting work on holidays, rule 757 and 759 allowing additional ordinary remission for work on holidays, read with the other provisions of Chapter XXI- on Remission, it is evident that, on the holidays and festival days, a convict prisoner is generally exempted from work. But he is not entitled to the benefit of remission for such exemption from work. However if he is required to work on holidays he is entitled to a few days of additional ordinary remission only, which is again subject to the maximum limit. 

 a) That no prisoner with a sentence not exceeding two months shall be on titled to any such remission; 

 186. 31.08: Thus in consideration of the legal status of the Circular dated 21.05.1959 as an existing law allowing remission on account of blood donation and the certificate of সন্ধানী about the donation of blood by the incumbent MP on 13 dates and the report of the jail authority as quoted above, it is held that the incumbent MP is entitled to remission of 486 days as calculated by him, of course, subject to the maximum limit allowable to him. His calculation is correct as per the Circular dated 21.05.1959 

 209. On the other hand, a news item was published in ‘the daily Prothom Alo’ on 10.05.2014 having a title “সাজা কম খেটেই বেরিয়ে যান সংসদ”. As per the news report, after the judgment being pronounced, the respondent No.7 surrendered to the Court on 14.09.2000 and accordingly he was sent to the Jail on the same day. It was also reported that he has been freed from the Jail on 01.12.2005 after serving 5 years 2 months and 17 days in Jail as Koyedi. As per the said news report, earlier the respondent No.7 had been in hajot for the instant case for a period of 4 months and 24 days but surprisingly as per the Koyed Register, it (hajotbas) was shown as 3 years 2 months and 25 days, which is illegal. The respondent No.7 had suffered both in hajot and Jail for a total period of 5 years 7 months and 21 days. It was reported that the duration of period of conviction of the respondent No.7 was reduced to 1 year 6 months and 17 days. In that context, it was reported that the respondent No.7 became free before 2 years 10 months and 1 day left of his actual exit date from Jail. It was also mentioned worthy that the Senior Super of the Chittagong Jail observed that it was a serious fraud made by the accused-convicted. 

 233. Respondent No.10 appeared and filed affidavit. In compliance of the show cause notice it is stated that the said news item (Annexure-2), the reporter took some snaps of relevant parts of Koyed Register where necessary information lies as evidence of his news. In respect of the statements made in paragraph Nos.1-9 of Affidavit-of-compliance dated 09.09.2014 are matters of record except the re-joinder (প্রতিবাদ-লিপি) dated 10.05.2014 made by respondent No.9 & the statement ‘গত ০১.০৭.২০১৪ খ্রিষ্টাব্দ তারিখ প্রথম আলো পত্রিকার চট্টগ্রাম অফিসের সিনিয়র রিপোর্টার জনাব একরামুল হকের লিখিত আবেদনের প্রেক্ষিতে নিম্মস্বাক্ষরকারী প্রদত্ত যে সকল তথ্য’ respondent No.10 (Annexure-5 series) of Affidavit-of-compliance এর মাধ্যমে মহামান্য আদালতে উপস্থাপন করেছেন, তা সঠিক নয়। made by the respondent No.9 in his report dated 03.09.2014 and hence, the respondent No.10 has no comment except to state that the respondent Nos.8 & 9 are to put to strict proof thereof. The respondent No.10 didn’t receive the re-joinder (প্রতিবাদ-লিপি) dated 10.05.2014 made by respondent No.9 to be published in ‘the daily Prothom Alo’. It is further stated that the respondent No.9, regarding the service of the period of sentence in Jail by the Respondent No.7, Nizam Uddin Hazari, admitted in his re-joinder (প্রতিবাদ-লিপি) dated 10.05.2014 that ‘রেয়াত প্রায় সাজা ভোগ শেষে তিনি ০১.১২.২০০৫ খ্রি: তারিখ অত্র কারাগার হতে মুক্তি লাভ করেন’(Annexure-X1 to Affidavit-of-compliance dated 09.09.2014) which is a focal basis to the news item dated 10.05.2014 with regard to statement ‘গত ০১.০৭.২০১৪ খ্রিষ্টাব্দ তারিখ প্রথম আলো পত্রিকার চট্টগ্রাম অফিসের সিনিয়র রিপোর্টার জনাব একরামুল হকের লিখিত আবেদনের প্রেক্ষিতে নিম্মস্বাক্ষরকারী প্রদত্ত যে সকল তথ্য’respondent No. 10 Annexure-5 series of Affidavit of compliance- এর মাধ্যমে মহামান্য আদালতে উপস্থাপন করেছেন, তা সঠিক নয়।’(Annexure-X1 to Affidavit-of-Compliance dated 09.09.2014 page-9), the deponent begs to state that this statement is false, misleading and suppression of facts as Annexure-5 series of Affidavit-of-compliance dated 07.07.2014 filed on behalf of respondent No.10 are photocopies of snaps of concerned original koyed Register where lies some necessary information relating to the service of the period of sentence in Jail by the respondent No.7, Nizam Uddin Hazari. 

 250. He next submits that after the publication of the aforesaid news item dated 10.05.2014, neither the respondent No.7 nor Chittagong Central Jail Authority denied the allegations or information made in the news item; or sent any re-joinder (প্রতিবাদ-লিপি) against the news item to Prothom Alo; which establishes the authenticity of content of the news item, but after filing of the present writ petition the respondent No.9 has stated, “গত ১০/০৫/২০১৪ খ্রিঃ তারিখ দৈনিক প্রথম আলো পত্রিকায় ‘সাজা কম খেটেই বেরিয়ে যান সংসদ’ প্রকাশিত বক্তব্য সঠিক নহে” Which is nothing but an ill motivated trial to run the original fact into another direction. The respondent No.10 didn’t receive the rejoinder (প্রতিবাদ-লিপি) dated 10.05.2014 made by the respondent No.9 to be published in ‘the daily Prothom Alo’. The respondent No.9 regarding the service of the period of sentence in jail by the respondent No.7, Nizam Uddin Hazari, admitted in his re-joinder (প্রতিবাদ-লিপি) dated 10.05.2014 that, “রেয়াত প্রথায় সাজা ভোগ শেষে তিনি ০১/১২/২০০৫ খ্রিঃ তারিখ অত্র কারাগার হতে মুক্তি লাভ করেন” which is a focal basis to the news item dated 10.05.2014. 

 765. Special remission may be given to any prisoner whether entitled to ordinary remission or not, other than a prisoner undergoing a sentence referred to in Rule 752, for special services, as for example: 

 5. If the person making the application on enquiry is found to be an interloper who interferes with the action of any person or authority as above which does not concern his is not entitled to make such petition. 

 “Mr. S.R. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court were wrong in deciding the disputed question of facts relating to title to the land which could only have been done by taking proper evidence, oral and documentary. Whether the relinquishment by Hiralal Mukherjee, Manager of Ramgarh Tea Estate in whose favour the land was originally settled legally transferred title in favour of the Union Agency Ltd. depended on the decision as to whether a registered document was necessary to effect the relinquishment. The learned Counsel also submitted that the decision as to whether the Union Agency Ltd. was a part and parcel of the appellant-company required investigation into facts. It appears that the High Court did not believe the genuineness of the rent receipt dated 25.3.67 produced by the appellant-company in support of its claim that rent was being paid by the company to the Government and it also found discrepancies with respect to the Khatian number mentioned in the rent receipt. The land in dispute was recorded as Khatian No.1/36 after the mutation case No.2/1, whereas the rent receipt showed that rent was being paid in respect of land in Khatian No.1/38. Further, there was no reason as to why the appellant-company whose name was not recorded in the Khatian should pay rent in respect of the land of which M/s. Union Agency Ltd. was the recorded tenant. The questions raised by the learned Counsel relate to the title of the appellant-company which depend on facts which are in dispute and can only be settled after full evidence has been properly taken. Mr. Sultan Hossain Khan, the learned Deputy Attorney General who appeared on behalf of the Government also conceded that where facts are disputed; the High Court, in exercising jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution should not proceed to settle the disputed facts requiring taking of evidence. There is a long line of decisions in favour of the view that the High Court should not enter into disputed questions of fact nor decide any question as to title which require investigation into facts and taking of elaborate evidence.” 

 351. The proceeding under Art. 102(2) of the Constitution is a summary one and it is decided on the statements made on affidavits filed by the parties and the documents annexed to the application and the affidavit-in-opposition. Hence it is often held that the court will decline to exercise jurisdiction when the application involves resolution of disputed question of fact. The decision reported in 42 DLR(AD) 13 lends support to the above contention. In this summary proceeding examination of disputed question of fact which is a complicated in nature and as a general rule cannot be undertaken nor investigation of title to property made and it is neither desirable nor advisable to enter into the merit and record a finding as to disputed question of fact. The decision reported in 51 DLR (AD) 232 lends support to the above order. The court will neither decide the complicated question of title nor disputed questions of fact relating to damages or compensation.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-35 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 11-9-2006 passed by the District Judge, Comilla in Title Appeal No.196 of 1997 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 24-8-1997 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla in Civil Suit No. 132 of 1994 dismissing the suit should not be set-aside. 

 2. Facts relevant for disposal of the rule are that the petitioner Nos. 1-2, 12-14 and the predecessor of the petitioner Nos.3-11 as plaintiffs instituted Civil Suit No. 118 of 1988 subsequently (re-numbered as Civil Suit No. 132 of 1994) before the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla for declaration of Title alleging that the suit land appertaining to CS Khatian No.11 corresponding to Hal Khatian No. 40 of Mouja Porkara under Police Station Chowddagram originally belonged to Dula Mia and his brother namely-Sekandar Ali with equal 8 annas share, for arrears of rent superior landlord obtained decree in rent suit without serving any notice and one Abdul Hakim shown to be auction purchaser. Abdul Hakim never obtained possession in pursuance of the decree passed in the rent suit. Dula Mia and his brother remained in possession of the suit property as before. Subsequently, Dula Mia filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 161 of 1939 for setting aside the auction and Abdul Hakim filed Civil Suit No. 19 of 1939 against Dula Mia and his brother Sekandar Ali and their mother for possession of the auction purchased land. Both the suits were disposed of in accordance with solenama and in terms of solenama 45 decimals of land were given settlement in favour of Sekandar Ali and Dula Mia from RS Plot No.415. Abdul Hakim Majumder settled 96 decimals of land by way of unregistered patta dated 15-10-1948 in favour of Dula Mia at Selami of Taka 145 but in the patta wrongly RS Plot No.415 written and possession was given on RS Plot No.1246 in favour of Dula Mia. Dula Mia remained in possession of the property under plot No.1246 entirely and 8 annas share of land under plot No.3 and paid rents for schedule Nos. 1, 2, 4, 6 and for half share of RS Plot No.415 of schedule No. 3. 

 3. During Revisional settlement SA Khatian No.40 was prepared in the name of Dula Mia and his brother Sekandar. Dula Mia died leaving the plaintiffs as heirs and the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. Sekandar Ali, brother of Dula Mia remained in possession of schedule No. 3 and transferred the property under schedule Nos.7-9 in favour of the plaintiffs by registered deed dated 2-1-1976. The defendants have no manner right, title and interest in the suit land. The defendants claimed title on the suit land on 15-7-1988, hence the suit. Subsequently, the plaintiffs brought an amendment of the plaint on 14-6-1995 and claimed title on adverse possession. 

 5. Sekandar Ali and Dula Mia never got settlement of 45 decimals of land equally and possessed accordingly. Sekandar Ali filed objection under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure against that execution case and that was dismissed on hearing and against that Appeal No.82 of 1943 was preferred by Sekandar Ali and that appeal was also disallowed on 17.08.1943. The claim of the plaintiff is that he obtained 96 decimals of land by way of patta dated 15-10-1948 is quite false and fictitious. Abdul Hakim Majumder never executed any patta deed in favour of Dula Mia. Plaintiff never obtained any suit property by way of Solenama and also did not obtain any property by registered deed dated 2-1-1976. The claim of the plaintiff is quite false and fictitious. The predecessor of the defendant Abdul Hakim obtained the suit property by auction purchase and obtained possession and during their possession the plaintiff and Sekandar Ali trespassed into the land comprising 19 decimals under plot Nos. 360 and 361 and subsequently got registered deed dated 25-6-1976 from the defendant No.1 and obtained possession of 6 decimals of land. Abdul Hakim Majumder filed Title Suit No.57 of 1988 for recovery of khas possession of 13 decimals of land in the court of Nangalkot and the suit of the plaintiff is liable to be dismissed. 

 7. After hearing, the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla dismissed the suit of the plaintiff against which appeal was preferred which was also disallowed by the appellate court in Title Appeal No.196 of 1997. 

 10. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that both the courts below, though dismissed the suit of the plaintiff with the concurrent findings that the plaintiffs could not prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence that they have title and possession in the suit land but this findings are based on non-consideration of the oral and documentary evidence on record which were marked as exhibits. Thus, the Judgment and decree passed by the Courts below are not based upon the proper appreciation of the evidence on record. 

 15. He further submits that after institution of the suit for declaration of title the plaintiff by way of amendment prayed for a decree by way of adverse possession and in support of their claim PW 1 in his deposition and cross-examination asserted that their predecessor was in possession of the suit land by way of settlement and patta and they are in possession also and as a whole they are in possession about 60 years in the suit land. Other P.Ws. corroborated the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 and thus the plaintiffs proved their case that they are in possession in the suit land since CS operation and it was proved by the report of the Revenue Officer that the objection raised by the defendants was rejected as such the plaintiffs have been able to prove their case. On the other hand, the defendants though produced some documents before the court but by adducing oral evidence they could not prove their possession in the suit land. Both the courts below on mis-appreciation of the facts and circumstances of the case mis-construed the same and arrived at a wrong decision in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff by which committed an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 16. On the other hand, Mr Md Israfil Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties submits that the plaintiff-petitioners could not prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence on record before the trial court and the trial court on proper perusal of the evidence on record and the documents exhibited by the parties found that the plaintiffs have no title and possession over the suit land and dismissed the suit of the plaintiff. The appellate court affirmed the Judgment and decree passed by the trial court in dismissing the suit with proper appreciation of the facts and circumstances of the case and the documents on record. Thus, the appellate court committed no error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 17. He further submits that the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below cannot be interfered with by the Revisional jurisdiction as there is no mis-reading of the evidence on record which mis-construed the facts of the case. He also submits that the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners could not prove their case in producing the documents before the Court, though the documents were filed before the Court and it was kept in safe custody but those were not examined or exhibited in the Court because those were forged and fabricated documents and, as such, the Courts below found that the plaintiff could not prove their case by adducing oral and documentary evidence that they have any title and possession in the suit land. 

 18. He further submits that the defendants by adducing oral and documentary evidence prove their case that they have title and possession in the suit land, as they have got possession through Court, the defendant also established their claim that the alleged un-registered patta has no existence at all and on consideration of this fact both the Courts below found title and possession of the defendants in the suit land. So, the claim of the plaintiffs of adverse possession is not established in any form of evidence both oral and documentary and on consideration the aforesaid oral and documentary evidence of the trial court and the appellate court concurrently found that the defendants are in possession on the suit land and the plaintiffs have no title and possession on the suit land and dismissed the suit as well as the appeal. Thus, the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below cannot be interfered with by the Revisional jurisdiction in the facts and circumstances of the case. He prayed for discharged of the Rule. 

 20. Title Suit No.132 of 1994 (re-numbered) was filed for declaration of title as well as adverse possession. The trial court framed 4 issues:-1) whether the suit is maintainable in its present form? 2) Whether the suit is barred by limitation? 3) Whether the plaintiffs have title over the suit land? 4) Whether the plaintiffs have possession in the suit land? 

 21. On perusal of the record it appears that the predecessor of the Plaintiff-Petitioners namely Dula Mia and his brother namely Sekander Ali were the original owners of the suit land evidencing from the CS Khatian (Exhibit-1(Ka)) and RS Khatian (Exhbit-1). The predecessor of the Plaintiff-Petitioners filed Miscellaneous Case No. 161 of 1939 for settlement. The predecessor of the Defendants-Opposite Parties No. 1-3 instituted Civil Suit No. 19 of 1939 for recovery of khas possession. The suit was decreed on 11-10-1939 on Solenama (Exhibit-2) according to Solenama, 0.45 acre were settled to Dula Mia and Sekender Ali. As per terms of Solenama Suit land was settled to Dula Mia vide registered patta dated 15-10-1948 and Partly Settlement Khatian No. 151 was recorded for Dula Mia and after SAT Act coming into force, Dula Mia became owner of the Suit land under the Government and RS Khatian (Exhibit-1) was recorded in the name of Dula Mia and he paid rents (Exhibit-3 series). 

 24. The plaintiffs pleaded adverse possession in Title Suit No. 118 of 1988 (present suit) in paragraph No.5 as follows: 

 (iv) The dismissal of the suit being Title Suit No. 57 of 1988 filed by the defendant-predecessors for recovery of possession of 13 decimals of land of plot o. 361 appertaining khatian No. 40 for the predecessor of the plaintiffs shows that possession remained with plaintiff predecessor. (v) The successors of Abdul Hakim Majumder i.e. the defendants in the present suit filed objection under Rule 30 of the Tenancy rules against record of rights in the name of the plaintiffs and for correcting the record in the name of the defendants. The Revenue Officer by an order dated 06-8-1990 dismissed the objection with the finding as follows: 

 30. AK Fazlul Haque Majumder, son of late Abdul Hakim Majumder filed Title Suit No. 57 of 1988 against Ayub Ali and others sons of Dula Mia in the court of Assistant Judge, Nangolkot, Comilla for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of 13 decimals of land in plot no. 361 appertaining to khatian No.40 (part of the suit land) which was contested by the defendant in that suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation in the plaint. The plaintiff of that suit did not proceed with the suit as a result the suit was dismissed due to absence of the plaintiff, Ext. Ka/5(Kha) vide order dated 21-9-1991 of the learned Assistant Judge, Nangolkot, Comilla. 

 33. In the Case reported in 54 DLR (AD) 173 relying on the case reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287 and other decisions it has been held by our Apex Court "Since the receipt is not a document of title it could not canter title to the plaintiff under the provisions of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act but the uninterrupted adverse and hostile possession of the plaintiff over a period of 12 years The plaintiff has acquired title by adverse possession. 

 34. Then in paragraph 10 it has been held by Appellate Division as follows: "Thus when there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferor. If he continues in possession of immovable property for more that twelve years he will acquire an indefeasible title. 

 36. In the present case if it is found that the patta granting settlement in favour of the plaintiffs predecessor is defective then in view of continues adverse possession of the plaintiffs from their predecessors for more than 60 years prior to the institution of the suit as evidenced form the rent receipts and oral and documentary evidence has conferred indefeasible title on the plaintiffs. 

 37. In the case reported in 6 MLR (AD) 257 the Appellate Division in paragraph held; "The court of appeal below on consideration of the evidence on record held that in view of the possession of the plaintiffs since 1926 ad that Jogendra did not transfer the property for and on behalf of Ananda, the minor and thus the transfer was invalid one and that it is proved on admitted evidence that the plaintiffs are in possession of the disputed properties for more than 12 years before the institution of the suit and that Baisnab was in possession all along and that the plaintiffs were in possession on the date of the filing of the suit and was also in possession for more than 12 years before the institution of the suit and thus perfected their title in respect of the suit properties by adverse possession against the defendants and all others." 

 38. In the present case the plaintiffs have been able to prove their possession and their predecessors' possession since the time of CS record and hence, even if there is any defect in the transfer of title to the plaintiffs they are entitled to declaration of title by adverse possession of more than 60 years of the date of the institution of the suit. 

 41. In the present case, since the unregistered patta was accompanied by delivery of possession the lease is valid for one year and the plaintiffs and their predecessors having continued in possession with the assent of the lessor the plaintiffs became tenants by holding over under section 116 of the Transfer of property Act. So even if the unregistered patta is treated as lease for one year, lease continued by the possession of the plaintiffs and their predecessors and therefore, they became tenants in the suit land by holding over under section 116 of the Transfer of property Act. Hence, the settlement in favour of the plaintiffs' predecessor is valid and the plaintiffs being in lawful possession has acquired title in the suit land. 

 50. From the discussions made above and the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, the order sheet of the trial court and other documents produced before the Court, it appears that the plaintiffs have title and possession in the suit land and they have also acquired title by way of adverse possession in the suit land, since they are enjoying uninterrupted possession in the suit land and CS Record and SA Record and rent receipts and the order of the Revenue Officer in the mutation case proved the aforesaid claim of the plaintiffs. Thus, the Courts below committed an error of law in dismissing the suit of the plaintiffs which occasioned a failure of justice. Thus, the Rule succeeds. 

 52. The impugned judgment and decree dated 11-9-2006 passed by the District Judge, Comilla in Title Appeal No.196 of 1997 affirming the judgment and decree dated 24-8-1997 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla in Civil Suit No.132 of 1994 are set aside. Accordingly, the title suit No. 132 of 1994 is decreed.

4. It is stated that Mrs. Inge Flatz on 25-6- 1984 executed a new Power of Attorney in favour of one Mohsin Darbar son of late Dawodbhai Darbar, a member of Bohra Community as lawful attorney to do all such acts as embodied in the said instrument including the sale of the property. On 10-8-1985 an agreement for sale was executed acknowledging the part payment between Mrs lnge Flatz through her' attorney and the plaintiff and possession was handed over to him along with all the original documents relating to the title of the property. Manzur Ahmed, (the plaintiff) filed the suit for specific performance of contract on 23-1-1993 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka being Title Suit No.14 of 1993, renumbered as Title Suit No.179 of 1999. 

 5. The plaintiff stated that in the agreement for sale the price was fixed at 60,000 sterling pound and Mrs Inge Flatz received an advance of 20,000 sterling pound and the plaintiff promised to pay the balance amount of the price at the time of registration of the sale deed, either in cash or through bank from income of the plaintiff originated in the United Kingdom. Since the vendor did not take steps for obtaining income tax clearance certificate and permission to sell the suit property which amounts to refusal to execute and register the sale deed, the plaintiff was compelled to file the suit. 

 6. Defendant No.3, RAJUK filed written statement stating that the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree on the following grounds: 

 20. If the plaintiff is to establish his personal right to an office which would entitle him to possession of the property in suit, on his death either during the pendency of the suit or during the pendency of appeal, the right to sue will not survive and the suit would abate. This means, in cases where the relief sought is ultimately connected with the individuality of the deceased, the right to sue will not survive against his legal representatives. To make the point more clear, there are certain types of wrongs which, though a remedy for them is available against the wrongdoer during his lifetime, does not permit of a remedy for them against his representatives after the death. Under the English law an executor represents the debts and the property of his testator but not his person. It is in general true of the position of a legal representative in our country, 

 23. The question of abatement of whole suit depends on whether the defendant was such a necessary party that his absence would result in the dismissal of the whole suit. However, if the deceased was a proper party the suit would not abate as a whole. It depends upon the facts of each case. Reference may be made in this connection are the cases reported in AIR 1928 Lah 572 (FB) and Nasir Mohammad vs Hamid Ali Chowdhury, Civil Petition No. 227 of 1995 reported). In the above unreported case in a suit for specific performance, a person subsequently entered into contract with the vendor. Vendor died and his legal representatives were not brought on record and the suit abated against the heirs of the vendor and it resulted in abatement of the suit as whole as the suit was not maintainable against a person who had not acquired title from the vendor. The question whether the whole appeal abates or only a part of it because of appellant's failure to bring on record within the time the legal representatives of the deceased shall be decided in each case on facts of the Case. If a decree Can be passed and given effect to in. so far as the rights of the parties actually before the court are ,concerned without interfering with the rights of others, the appeal 'fan continue, if not, it abates as a whole, 

 Therefore the judicial proceedings in the hereditary case were terminated on the 4th of .' October 1985 by the transfer of the title to Karim Franz Solaiman (see attached copy)." 

 37. He also drew our attention to the notarial certificates of the said document, the birth and death certificates of Mrs Inge Flatz. In birth and death certificates the date of birth was clearly mentioned in English as '03-6-1941' and the date of death as '30-3-1985'. In the original death certificate also it was written in German, English; French and some other languages. In that certificate the decea Sed's parents names and all particulars have been mentioned. This certificate was also duly authenticated by a notary public. 

 39. Section 78 prescribes-special modes of proving the contents of various kinds of official 'documents; public acts, proceedings of the legislature etc. Clause (6) relates to the proof of documents of any other class in a foreign country by the original, or by a copy certified by the legal keeper thereof, with a certified under the seal of a notary public, or of a Bangladesh Consul or diplomatic agent, that the copy is duly certified by the officer having the legal custody of the original, and upon proof of the character of the document according to the law of the foreign country." 

 40. This clause requires three conditions to be fulfilled for reception of public documents in a foreign country. A public document in a foreign country should be certified by the legal keeper of the original documents, or of a Consul General and there shall be proof of the character of the document according to the law of the foreign  country. These copies were duly certified by the keeper of the documents with certificates under the seal of a notary public. This clause lays down three conditions for admitting public documents of the nature but the admission of judicial record is not a condition precedent for drawing the requisite presumption under section 86 of the Evidence Act. Except the birth and death certificates, other documents are from the judicial record. In the hereditary proceedings the date of death of loge Flatz had been mentioned as 30-3-1985 and this date corroborates the date mentioned in the death certificate which is, also a public document. Therefore conditions laid downin clause (6) of section 78 have been fulfilled and there is nolegal bar to admit them in evidence. 

 "It is not disputed that the copy of the judgment is certified by the legal keeper of the original within the meaning of S.78(6) of the Evidence Act; nor is it contended that there is no certificate under the seal, of an . Indian Consul certifying that the copy is certified by the officer having the legal custody of the original. But what is contended is that under S.78(6) of the Evidence Act three conditions must be complied with before the judgment can De admitted in evidence and the third condition, namely; proof of character of the document according to the law of the foreign country, is not forthcoming in this case. A perusals. 78(6) of the Evidence Act makes it clear that apart from the two certificates one by the legal keeper of the original documents and the other by the Consul General there shall also be proof of the character of the document according to the law of the foreign country before the document is admitted. "It is a condition 'precedent. The short question, therefore, is whether there is such proof in this case. Proof can be by direct or circumstantial evidence. Proof can also be given by placing before the Court facts giving rise to presumptions rebuttable or irrefutable. Section 86 of the Evidence Act lays down that a Court may presume the genuineness and accuracy of any document purporting to be a certified copy of any judicial record of any foreign country, if such a copy is duly certified in the manner and according to the rules in use in the country for certification of copies of judicial records. To give rise to this presumption it is not necessary that the judgment of the foreign country should have already been admitted in evidence. While S. 78(6) of the Evidence Act lays down three conditions for admitting the judgment in evidence, the admission of the judicial record is not a condition precedent for drawing the requisite presumption under S.86 of the Evidence Act. The presumption, may be drawn before the said record is admitted, The ascertaining whether there is the requisite certificate, viz., a certificate issued by any representative of the Central Government in the concerned country to the effect that the said document was certified in the manner Commonly in use in that country for the certificatory of copies of judicial record. If the distinction between the certificate and the judgment is borne in mind, the fallacy of the argument becomes apparent the requisite certificate makes the document admissible and not vice versa If there was such a certificate forthcoming in this case there is such a certificate the document may be presumed to be genuine and accurate. If it is presumed to be genuine and accurate, it shows its character, viz., that it is a genuine judgment made by the Supreme Court of New York. This is a fit case for raising the said presumption and with the aid of this presumption the third condition is also complied with i.e., it is a judgment of the Supreme Court of the State of New York made in accordance with law. As the three conditions laid down in 8.78(6) of the Evidence Act are fulfilled, the document can legitimately be admitted in evidence, and if it is admitted, the document; by its own force establishes that the aforesaid three conditions for the enforceability of the awards have been fulfilled." 

 44. A foreign public document may be proved by the original or a certified copy but in case of a certified copy it should be certified by the legal keeper of the document with a certificate by a notary public or of it diplomatic officer of Bangladesh to the effect that the copy is certified by the legal keeper of the original, and upon proof of the character of the document, S6 the condition is not of the contents but that the copy is certified by the keeper of the original. The first two conditions have been fulfilled, it has not been disputed that the keeper has not certified the copies. There are notarial certificates to the effect that the copies were issued by the keeper. A diplomatic officer has authenticated them. Therefore the documents are presumed to be genuine and accurate. On fulfillment of these conditions there is no doubt about the character of the same. The mode of proof of public documents mentioned in section 78 is permissive, and therefore, the court is not precluded from having the other modes of proof. A public document may be proved by production of the original or by a certified copy under section 77 or in the manner prescribed in section 78. A foreign judicial record is a public document and may be proved by a copy certified in the manner prescribed by sections 78(6) and 86 of the Evidence Act. Reference in this connection is Harand Chetlangia vs Ram Gopal Chetlangia, 27 1A 1 (PC)and AIR 1964 SC 538. 

 45. The. documents regarding the death of Mrs Inge Flats are relating to the judicial proceedings except the birth and death certificates but all those documents have been issued by the keeper thereof duly authenticated by the notary public and attested by the Embassy of Bangladesh. As regards the birth and death certificates these are clearly written in English and public documents. As mentioned above, the date of death of Inge Falatz has also been mentioned in the hereditary proceedings. Besides, the letter issued by the District Court of Bregenz was also in English. In this letter the Judge of the District. Court of Bregenz clearly mentioned that Mrs Inge Flatz died on 30-3-1985, leaving a son and husband. This English letter was also duly countersigned, by the President of the court and also attested by the Embassy. From this letter which is in English we clearly 'find the date of death of Mrs Inge Flatz. This date tally with the date mentioned in the death certificate which is also in English and in the original death certificate it was also written in different languages including English. 

 63. A relief for specific performance being discretionary, the court is not bound to pass a decree even if the plaintiff proves the execution of the agreement for sale and payment of consideration unless and until the plaintiff comes in court with clean hands. Since from the very execution of the power of attorney is doubtful, and from the admission of the plaintiff that the defendant died at least at the initial stage of the suit, and if this admission is taken into consideration with the documents filed by the government, there is no doubt that Mrs Inge Flatz died long before the execution of the agreement for sale. Therefore, the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree for a specific performance on the strength of forged deeds. The High Court Division erred, therefore, in decreeing the suit for specific performance. 

 66. Apart from this, if these allegations are taken to be true that the petitioner Moudud Ahmed has secured the order of permission for his pecuniary gain, the deed of sale was admittedly executed in favour of Mrs Inge Flatz by the government who was the original lessee under the RAJUK. She had no relationship with Moudud Ahmed except that during the relevant time Moudud Ahmed was tenant under Mrs Inge Flatz. Mrs Inge Flatz did not transfer the property either in favour of Moudud Ahmed or in favour of his wife or his children. Mrs lnge Flatz executed an agreement for sale of the property in favour of Monjur Ahmed, brother of Moudud Ahmed, who is a citizen of England and has been residing in a separate mess.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 3137-3139 of 2013
parties:
Md. Harun-Ur-Rashid and others ------ Petitioners (in all the cases)
-Vs-
Md. Sirajul Islam and others ------ Respondents (In all the cases)
full_judgment:
3. The respondent Md. Sirajul Islam in these 3 Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal, as plaintiff, filed Title Suit No.134 of 1996 which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No.9.9 of 1997 in the Court of, the Assistant Judge, Nababgonj against the present leave-petitioners Md. Harun-Ur-Rashid and others and also the defendant-respondent Nos.2- 5 herein for permanent injunction. The leave-petitioners Md. Heron-Ur-Rashid and others also, as plaintiffs, filed Title Suit Nos.100 of 1997 and 101 of 1997 against Md. Sirajul Islam (the plaintiff of Title Suit No.99 of 1997). The Title Suit No.100 of 1997 was for declaration of title and the Title Suit No.101 of 1.997 was for a declaration that the judgment and decree dated 21.10.1995 passed in Title Suit No.254 of 1994 was fraudulent, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs. 

 4. The case of the plaintiff of Title Suit No.99 of 1997 (present-respondent No.1, Md. Sirajul Islam), in short, was that the suit land originally belonged to Khoda Boksha in 8 annas share and Sheikh Kalu and Sheikh Malu in 4 annas share each. Sheikh Malu died leaving behind 2 sons, Newazuddin and Mainuddin and 2 daughters Guljan and Nazibun Nessa. Thereafter, Newazuddin died leaving behind only son Romizuddin and a wife Keti Bibi. On 08.12.1966 Nazibun Nessa sold her 1.75 acres of land in favour of Keti Bibi. Thus: Keti Bibi and Romizuddin, by inheritance and by purchase, acquired 1.51 -acres of land from plot No.2721 and 2.31 acres of land from plot No.2792 and possessed that land exclusively by amicable partition. Romizuddin and Keti Bibi sold .8250 acre of land from plot No.2721 in favour of Zayeda Begum by kabala dated 19.02.1968 and since purchase, Zayeda Begum had been possessing the said land by paying rents. Keti Bibi died leaving behind only son Romizuddin. Romizuddin transferred 1.4550 acres of land in favour of the plaintiff by a kabala dated 06.12.1993. The plaintiff purchased .8250 acre of land also from Zayeda Begum by a registered kabala dated 08.10.1993. The plaintiff got possession of his purchased land and constructed 2 tin-shed huts on a portion of that purchased land and has been possessing the rest land by cultivation. That Romizuddin and Mainuddin threatened the plaintiff with dispossession in the year 1994 and as such the plaintiff filed Title Suit No.254 of 1994 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for declaration of title and that suit was decreed on 04.10.1995. On 14.06.1996 the defendants Md. Harun-Ur-Rashid and others tried to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land and hence the suit. 

 5. The case of the plaintiffs of Title Suit Nos.100 of 1997 and 101 of 1997 (the present leave-petitioners), in short, was that the suit plot No.2721 comprising 10.90 acres of land along with other lands originally belonged to Khoda Boksha in 8 annas share and Sheikh Kalu and Sheikh Malu in 4 annas share each. That Sheikh Malu died leaving behind 2 sons Mainuddin and Newazuddin and 2 daughters Guljan Bibi and Nazibun Nessa. Thereafter, Newazuddin died leaving behind a wife Keti Bibi and one son Romizuddin. That Mainuddin, Guljan Bibi, Nazibun Nessa, Romizuddin and Keti Bibi amicably partitioned their share in plot No.2721 and in S.A. Khatian their share comprising an area of 2.51 acres of land from plot No.2721 was duly record-ed. Romizuddin sold out .31 acre of land in favour of Mainuddin by a registered kabala dated 12.04.1966 and Mainuddin purchased another .1550 acre of land from said Romizuddin by a registered kabala dated 15.06.1966. Thus Mainuddin acquired 1.57 acres of land. Mamuddin sold out .33 acre of land to the plaintiffs by 3 separate registered kabalas dated 05.02.1987 and 09.02.1987. The plaintiffs got possession of their purchased land and they had been possessing the same peace-fully for more than 12 years. But suddenly on 06.05.1994 the defendants Md. Sirajul Islam and others threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession; that it was then disclosed that the defendant No. 1 filed Title Suit No.254 of 1994 against Romizuddin and others and managed a collusive and fraudulent decree and on the basis of that decree the defendant has threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession and hence the suits. 

 6. All the above 3 Title Suit Nos.9-9 of 1997, 100 of 1997 and 101 of 1997 were tried analogously by the learned Assistant Judge, Nababgonj (Sadar), Dhaka. The trial court, or consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties, decreed Title Suit No.99 of 1997 for permanent injunction and dismissed both Title Suit Nos.100 of 1997 and 101 of 1997. As against this analogous judgment and decree of the trial court the present leave petitioners filed Title Appeal Nos. 354 of 1997, 355 of 1997 and 356 of 1997 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. All those 3 title appeals were heard analogously by the learned. 

 7. Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka and by the analogous judgment and order dated 23.02.1999 the appellate court below dismissed all those 3 title appeals and thereby affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court. These leave-petitioners then preferred the above mentioned 3(three) Civil Revision Nos.1216 of 1999, 1217 of 1999 and 1218 of 1999 before the High Court Division and obtained rules. A Single Bench of the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and order, discharged all those rules making observations to the effect that the suit land i.e. .33 acre of land of suit plot No-2721 mentioned in the schedule to the plaint of Title Suit No.100 of 1997 is not specific and identifiable and it had also not been proved that this suit land of Title Suit No.100 of1997 is included in .82½ acre of suit land of Title Suit No.254 of 1994, that it was also not proved that .33 acre of-land as described in the schedule to the plaint of Title Suit No.101 of 1997 is they same land as described in the kabala of the plaintiff of that suit-the exhbits-UmaUma(2) and that the decree passed in Title Suit Nos:254 of 1994 still subsists and that Md. Sirajul Islam-the plaintiff of Title Suit No.99 of 1997 has been able to prove his title and possession in the suit land and that it was not proved al8o that .33 acre of land as claimed by the plaintiff of Title. Suit No.100 of 1997 is part of .824 acre of land as claimed by the plaintiff in Title Suit No.99 of 1997. 

 8. Mr. Qumrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate for the leave-petitioners has made submissions to the effect that the leave-petitioners Md. Harun-Ur-Rashid and others undisputedly, purchased .33 acre of land of the suit plot No.2721 from its rightful owner long before the purchase of the claimed land of the respondent Md. Sirajul Islam and in the circumstances the courts below committed wrong-and also injustice in dismissing the suit of the leave-petitioners for declaration of their title in their purchased .33 acre of land on a wrong finding that this suit land has not been well specified. The learned Advocate has argued also that there is no clash in between the leave- petitioners and the respondent Md. Sirajul Islam as regards title in their respective claimed land and in the circumstances the courts below ought to have decreed the suit of these leave-petitioners for declaration of their title in their claimed .33 acre of land. 

 9. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate for the respondents has made submissions to the effect that in a suit for declaration of title the plaintiff requires to specify the suit land clearly, but in this suit all the courts below found that the claimed .33 acre of land of the plaintiffs Md. Harun-Ur-Rashid and others has not been well specified in the plaint and that the demarcation of this suit land which has been given in the plaint did not tally with the demarcation mentioned in the purchase deeds of the plaintiffs. The learned Senior Advocate has argued that in the circumstance the courts below rightly dismissed the suits filed by these leave-petitioners. 

 11. It appears that all the 3 courts have found that in Title Suit No.100 of 1997 filed by these present leave-petitioners the suit land was not well demarcated and that the specification of this suit land which the plaintiffs mentioned in their plaint did not tally with the specification of the land mentioned in their purchase deed.
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

parties:
Nayeb Ali (Md) ------- Appellant
VS
Md Abdus Salam Khan being dead his heirs: 1(a) Md Mahafujur Rahman and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that Md Abdus Salam Khan (original respondent No. 1) as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 192 of 2000 before the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur against defendant No. 1-Md Nayeb Ali (appellant herein) stating, inter alia, that while the defendant owned and was in possession of the suit land, he entered into an agreement on 16-9-1999 to sell out 181/4 decimals land. The total value of the 181/4 decimals land was fixed at Taka 2,21,212 and the defendant received a sum of Taka 50,100 as baina money and.a bainapatra was executed by the defendant. It was settled that within 3-12-2000 the defendant would receive the remaining amount of Taka 1,71,112 and execute and register the sale deed. On several dates the defendant received total amount of Taka 1,24,000 .from the plaintiff and acknowledged the same on the bainapatra and handed over possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff and promised to execute and register the sale deed on 16-7-2000. Accordingly, the plaintiff went to the Sub-Registry Office on that date, but the defendant did not go there. On 6-8-2000 the plaintiff complained before the Koultia Union Parishad, but the defendant did not appear there. Hence, the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract. 

 6. Against the said judgment and decree passed by the trial Court defendant No. 1 preferred Title Appeal No. 242 of 2004 before the. learned District Judge, Gazipur and ultimately the appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur, who upon hearing the parties and considering the materials on record allowed the appeal, in part modifying the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, allowing specific performance in respect of 7 decimals land. 

 7. Being aggrieved the plaintiff filed Civil Revision No. 99 of 2006 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was made absolute thereby upholding the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Hence, defendant No. 1 as petitioner filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1102 of 2012 before this Division and leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner: "I. That in a suit for specific performance of contract there is no scope for deciding the question of title, but the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the deed of the wife of defendant No. 1 dated 19-10-1998 is hereby cancelled, void and inoperative and not acted upon. II. That in a suit for specific performance of contract the real question is whether the contract between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 is genuine or not, whether the consideration money passed, but there is no scope to decide title over the suit land. In this case Sufia Khatun, the wife of defendant No. 1 is not a party, rather the date of the deed of heba-bil-awaz is 19-10-1998 and the alleged date of execution of the bainapatra dated 16-9-1999 was subsequent, and hence the High Court Division violated the settled principles and made out a third case and thereby erred in law in cancelling the registered heba-bil-awaz deed-No. 18423 dated 19-10-1998 and declaring the same as void and inoperative and not acted upon, as such the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is bad in law and the same is liable to be set-aside." 

 9. Mr SM Masud Hossain Dolon, learned Advocate appearing for respondent Nos. 1 (a)-1(e), who were substituted in place of respondent No.1, Abdus Salam Khan, made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He also submitted that the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is a proper judgment reversing the judgment of the appellate Court. He submitted that the learned Additional District judge committed serious error of law in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Joint District Judge and occasioned failure of justice. He lastly submitted that the learned Additional District Judge passed the impugned judgment and decree without perusing the materials on record and failed to appreciate the question of title is immaterial in a suit for specific performance of contract and committed error of law occasioning failure of justice. 

 13. The appellate Court reversed the finding of the trial Court upon finding that defendant No. 1 having earlier gifted 11 decimals land to his wife, the trial Court was wrong in decreeing the suit in respect of 18¼ decimals land, since the defendant no longer had title of the 11 decimals land which he had gifted to his wife. Accordingly the appellate Court awarded partial decree in respect of 7 decimals land.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Anowar Hossain, Advocate.……. For the petitioners.
Mr. Khair Ezaz Masud, Advocate..... For the opposite parties.
parties:
Md. Shajahan Bhuiyan and others …….. Petitioners.
Versus.
Md. Nurul Alam and others..…..Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
1. The Rule issued in this Civil Revision is about sustainability of the judgment and decree dated 14.06.2009 by which the learned Special District Judge, being the Nari-0-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal, Judge, Noakhali allowed Title Appeal No.57 of 2007 and thereby decreed Title Suit No. 30 of 1996 on reversing the judgment of dismissal dated 17.01.2007 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Hatiya, Noakhali in the said suit. 

 2. Plaintiffs’ Case: The plaintiffs filed the above noted Title Suit for the following four relieves: 

 (1) declaration of their title to the suit land comprising being 3 (three) parcels of land each measuring 1.50 acres i.e. a total of 4.50 acres as described in item Nos. 1, 2 and 3 of the Ka schedule to the plaint; 

 (2) declaration that the decree obtained by Oli Ullah, the predecessor of defendants Nos.1-8 in Title Suit No.210 of 1983 of the Court of Munsif, Hatiya, Nokhalia, is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs; 

 10. These defendants, in their joint written statement, deny plaintiffs’ right, title and possession. They contend that the suit is not maintainable, that it is barred by limitation and it also suffers from the defect of party. 

 12. The said D.S. recoded land diluvated as a result of river erosion but title of the D.S. tenant and also of Oli Ullah was never lost. But, in the Diara Jariap, the said D.S. recorded land was wrongly shown as part of Block Dag Nos.4262 and 4261 and both these two plots were included in Mouja Bora Dail. The draft khatian for both the plots were recorded in the name of Oli Ullah, but the final khatian was wrongly prepared in the name of the Government as khas khatian No.1. 

 13. So Oli Ullah filed Title suit No.210 of 1983 against the Government and obtained an ex-parte decree. Thereafter Oli Ullah obtained Mutation Khatian No.398 for his 7.31 acres and the Government functionarises have identified the said 7.31 acres as 7 sub-plots under the said two Block Dags. 

 17. However these defendants admit that Oli Ullah, being the predecessor of defendant Nos.1-8, obtained an ex-parte decree in Title Suit No.210 of 1983 and that pursuant to the said decree the Revenue office opened Mutation Khatin No.398 for 7.31 acres out of the land of the two Block Dag Nos. 4262 and 4261. 

 18. Proceeding and decisions of the courts below: The trial court framed 5 issues on (1) maintainability of the suit, (2) limitation, (3) defect of party, (4) plaintiffs’ right, title and possession over the suit land and (5) the relieves prayed for by the plaintiffs. 

 22. Upon consideration of the evidence on record, the trial court delivered its first judgment dated 17.01.2004 and decreed the suit. Against that judgment the defendants Nos.9 and 10 preferred Title Appeal No. 28 of 2004 in which the learned Joint District Judge, by his judgment dated 16.07.2005 recorded a finding that the suit land had diluvaled and reappeared. However the said court set aside the judgment of the trial court and sent the original suit back on remand with specific direction to cause a local investigation for the purpose of ascertaining the identity of the suit land with the D.S. recorded land. 

 25. Deliberation at the hearing in Revision: Mr. Md. Anowar Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner-defendants, submits that the predecessor of the defendants Oli Ullah obtained an exparte decree in Title Suit No.210 of 1983 with regard to his title and that the defendant Nos.9 and 10, as his successor-in-interest, proved their title in the instant suit by producing all the title documents, namely the D.S. khatian, the unregistered patta dated 28.01.1931 executed by D.S. tenant Zinnat Ali, the rent receipts showing payment of rent by Oli Ullah to the D.S. tenant and other subsequent documents. 

 30. Mr. Masud, the learned Advocate, next submits that in the first time appeal being Title Appeal No. 28 of 2004 the appellate court in its judgment dated 16.07.2005 recorded a clear finding that the suit land firstly diluvated and then re-appeared and that in the Diara Jariap the Government functionaries identified the suit land and other lands as part of two larger plots being Block Dag Nos. 4161and 4162 and neither of the parties challenged that finding in a Revision and therefore the trial court was bound by that finding but the trial court failed to consider this legal aspect. 

 32. Mr. Masud, the learned Advocate, next submits that since the D.S. plot Nos. 1657 and 1658 as claimed by the defendants had diluvated, it has vested with the Government by virtue of the amended section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (the SAT Act, 1950) and the Government has legal authority to lease out the same and accordingly the plaintiffs lawfully acquired their title by virtue of the lease deeds in 1978-1979. 

 34. Mr. Masud, the learned Advocate, next submits that the defendants’ predecessor obtained the disputed ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 210 of 1983 without impleading the plaintiffs as parties, although the plaintiffs had acquired title before institution of the suit and therefore the decree is not binding upon the plaintiffs. 

 35. Mr. Masud, the learned Advocate lastly submits that the plaintiffs could prove their title and possession by producing sufficient oral and documentary evidence and that the appellate court legally passed the impugned judgment and decree and therefore the Rule should be discharged. 

 39. The record of Title Suit No.210 of 1983 instituted by defendants’ predecessor Oli Ullah was called for. The plaint of this suit shows that Oli Ullah, as the plaintiff had clearly admitted that the suit land had diluvated and re-appeared. He has stated as follows: 

 48. Section 86 of the Act, 1950 clearly provides that a land that has diluvated before the of P.O No. 135 of 1972 (i.e. after April 1956) or that will diluvate in future shall vest in the Government. It follows that irrespective of what ever title or right was acquired by Oli Ullah from the D.S. recorded tenant Zinnat Ali by virtue of the unregistered patta dated 28.1.1931 (Exhibit-ka) and the three rent receipts for the years 1341 to 1362 D.S (Exhibit-Ga-series) it had extinguished as a result of diluvion that took place some time before 1965 i.e. before the Diara Map. It follows that the Government has acquired lawful right to lease out the land that was earlier recorded as D.S. plot No.1657 and 1658. 

 51. It is in evidence that the plaintiffs were given permanent settlement of the land by the Government out of the Block Dag Nos.4261 and 4262 in the year 1978-79 by the three lease document (Exhibit-1-3) for the lands of three Khas Mohal plot Nos. 21153, 21154 and 21154/1 of Mouja Burir Char It follows that the plaintiffs were necessary parties in Title Suit No.210 of 1983 which was instituted by Olli Ullah in 1983 claiming 7.31 acres of land of D.S. plot No. 1657 and 1658 corresponding to Block Dag Nos. 4261 and 4262. Because the plaintiffs were already in the scenario as lessees since 1978-79. But the suit was filed only against the Government. So the decree passed in that suit is not binding upon the plaintiffs so far their interest is concerned. 

 54. The appellate court has independently discussed and assessed the oral and documentary evidence produced by both sides and also considered the finding earlier recorded by the appellate court in the 1st Judgment dated 16-07-2005 in the first time appeal being Title Appeal No. 28 of 2004 by which the original suit was sent back on remand. 

 56. The appellate court correctly found that in the earlier T.S. No. 210 of 1983, the present plaintiffs as lessees under the Government since 1978-1979 were necessary parties, but they were not made parties and therefore the exparte decree passed therein will not affect plaintiffs title to the suit land. 

 58. In view of the above I hold that plaintiffs have been able to prove their right, title and possession over the suit land measuring 4.50 acres. They could also prove their claim with regard to the ex-parte decree and the Mutation opened in the name of the defendants predecessor Oli Ullah. However that decree is binding on the government but excluding the land of the plaintiffs. 

 59. The trial court misread the direction of the appellate court as recorded in the judgment dated 16.07.2005 passed in the first time Title Appeal No. 28 of 2004 and erroneously found that “there was neither scope nor justification of obtaining settlement of the suit land by the plaintiffs in the year 1979……”. The trial court without properly considering the pleadings as a whole and the evidence on record and erroneously found that (the Government) “defendant Nos. 11-13 have specifically denied such alluvion and diluvion of the suit land”.

parties:
Sree Monohar Chandra Biswas & others .....Petitioners.
Vs.
Sreemati Laxmi Rani Sikder & others. ....Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
1. The Rule issued in this Civil Revision is about sustainability of the judgment and decree dated 26-01-1998 by which the learned Additional District Judge, Magura allowed Title Appeal No. 182 of 1996 and thereby dismissed Title Suit No. 89 of 1994 on reversing the judgment and decree dated 7-10-1996 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mahammadpur, Magura in the said suit in favour of the plaintiff-petitioners. 

 (1) declaration of their title to and conformation of possession over the suit land measuring 20 decimals as described in the schedule to the plaint, 

 3. The plaintiffs claim that they have purchased the suit land by a kabala dated 07.06.1980 executed by the original owner Promotha Nath being the father of defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Since purchase, plaintiffs have been in continuous possession and paid rent to the Government. But, in the 1st part of Jasitha, 1401 B.S., the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs and to sell out the suit land. Later on, plaintiffs came to know that defendant Nos.1 and 2 have created a false and collusive transfer deed dated 27.07.1994 in favour of defendant No. 2(ka) being wife of defendant No.1 on the basis of a deed of gift dated 10.01.1979 purportedly executed by their father Promoth Nath in favour of one of his son being defendant No.2. Hence the suit. 

 5. This defendant admits the original ownership of Promoth Nath Sikder. But she denies title and possession of the plaintiffs by virtue of plaintiffs kabala dated 07-06-1980. She contends that the suit is not maintainable and that it is barred by limitation and bad for defect of party. 

 9. Mr. Roy, the learned advocate, further submits that the appellate court also failed to consider that the plaintiffs have produced sufficient and credible evidence to prove their title and possession and that the alleged deed of gift dated 10-01-1979 by the original owner in favour his son (defendant No.2) was never acted upon. 

 11. In reply Mr. Kalipada Mridha, the learned advocate for the opposite party defendant No. 2(ka), submits that the appellate Court, upon discussion of the oral and documentary evidence on record, rightly held that the deed of gift dated 10-01-1979 executed by the admitted owner Promoth Nath in favour of his son (defendant No.2) was a deed prior to that of plaintiffs’ kabala dated 27-06-1980 and therefore no title passed on to the plaintiffs. 

 14. Admittedly the suit land belonged to Promoth Nath which is further evidenced by the exparte decree obtained by Promoth Nath in Title Suit No. 461 of 1968 ( Exhibit-1-1(ka) in respect of correction of the S.A. record wrongly prepared in the names of one Mohiuddin and others. 

 15. Both the parties claim their title and possession as the successor-in-interest of the admitted owner Promoth Nath. The plaintiffs claim the suit land on the basis of the kabala dated 07.06.1980 (Exhibit-2) executed by Promoth Nath himself. On the other hand, claim of the defendant No.2(ka) is based on the gift deed that was executed by the same owner before the kabala of the plaintiffs i.e. by the deed of gift dated 10-01-1979 (Exhibit-ka) in favour of defendant No. 2 being the son of Promoth Nath. Defendant further claims that she purchased the suit land the kabala dated 27.07.1994 from the said son of Promotha Nath. 

 16. So the principal issue before this court is whether plaintiffs have acquired any title to the suit land by virtue of their kabala dated 07-06-1980 which is subsequent to the disputed deed of gift dated 10-01-1979 in favour of defendant’s vendor. 

 17. On this question of fact, the trial Court has endeavored to decide as to whether the respective title documents of the parties was acted upon and accordingly focussed its discussion on the possession aspect. 

 65. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 26-01-1998 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Magura in Title Appeal No. 182 of 1996 is hereby set aside. The judgment and decree dated 07-10-1996 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mohammadpur, Magura in Title Suit No. 89 of 1994 is hereby upheld with the modification in the order portion of the Judgment passed by the trial Court that the deed of gift dated 10-01-1979 executed by Promoth Nath in favour of defendant No. 2 Amal Kumar, so far it relates to the suit land, and the kabala dated 27-4-1974 executed by defendant No. 2 Amal Kumar in favour of defendant No. 2 (ka) Laximi Rani so far it relates to the suit land, are declared to be not binding upon the plaintiffs.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.1235 of 2011.
parties:
Moulvi Ali Ahmed being dead his heirs; 1(a) Kamal and others ------ Petitioners
 Versus
Ali Akbar and Another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Facts relevant for disposal of this petition are that respondent No.1 herein, as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.79 of 1998 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Kachua, Chandpur for Specific Performance of Contract impleading the predecessor in interest of the petitioners as defendant. 

 4. The trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 08.04.2001 decreed the suit. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendant filed Title Appeal No.49 of 2001 in the Court of District Judge, Chandpur. The appeal was filed by paying deficit Court fee and 30.10.2001 was fixed for supplying the deficit Court fee, on that date on the application of the appellant time was allowed up to 18.11.2001 to pay the deficit Court fee and again on 18.11.2001 the next date was fixed on 28.11.2001. And on this date the appellant did not take any step in the appeal and the same was dismissed for default. Thereafter, the defendant-appellant filed an application under Order XLI, rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure for re-admission of the appeal along with an application under section 5 of the limitation Act for condoning the delay in filing application out of time. The application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No.8 of 2002. The miscellaneous case was dismissed on 20.10.2010. Against the said order of dismissal of the miscellaneous case, the defendant-petitioner filed Miscellaneous Appeal No.261 of 2002 before the High Court Division. The appeal came up for hearing before a single bench of the High Court Division and the same was dismissed; hence this petition for leave to appeal. 

 6. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the nature of the suit, we are of the view that justice would be best served, if the appeal (Title Appeal No.49 of 2001) is restored to its original file and number with a cost of taka. 50,000.00 to the plaintiff-respondent No.1 to be paid by the petitioners. Accordingly, this petition is disposed of in the following terms: 

 The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division as well as the order dated 28.11.2001 dismissing Title Appeal No.41of 2001 are set aside. The Title Appeal No. 41 of 2001 is restored to its file and number. It further appears that an application was filed before the High Court Division for transposition but that was not disposed of on merit as the appeal was dismissed. However, if so advised, the concerned respondent may renew the prayer before the Appellate Court. It further appears that the deficit Court fee was not paid before the Appellate Court. The petitioner is directed to pay the deficit Court fee, within 2 (two) months from the date of receipt of this judgment and also the cost of taka 50,000.00 within the said period. The amount of cost shall be deposited to the trial Court. Thereafter, the plaintiff shall be at liberty to withdraw the cost (taka 50,000.00) as per his own convenience. The Appellate Court is further directed to dispose of the appeal expeditiously.
